currentContext.business: Fine Organics manufactures performance speciality additives derived almost entirely from sustainable, plant-based feedstock, supplying critical ingredients to manufacturers across diverse industries. Its technologically advanced portfolio spans high-performance food emulsifiers, advanced polymer additives, premium personal care ingredients and highly specialised feed nutrition solutions, each purpose-built to solve a specific manufacturing challenge such as improving processing efficiency in bioplastics, enhancing texture and mouthfeel while maintaining clean-label standards, or improving the safety and sustainability profile of end-user products. The Company exports its solutions worldwide and supports them through an integrated network of regional distributors and specialised technical support teams.

currentContext.expansion: The sections routed here (MD&A industry overview, Board's Report and the AGM Notice) do not describe any company capex programme, capacity addition or project timeline. The only expansion-related disclosure is structural: as on March 31, 2026 the Company had five subsidiaries — Fine Organics (USA), Inc., Fine Organics Europe BV, Fine Organic Industries (SEZ) Private Limited, Fine Organics Americas LLC and Fine Organics FZE — and two joint venture companies, Fine Zeelandia Private Limited and Fine Organic Industries (Thailand) Co., Ltd. risks.risk: Climate change and crop-linked feedstock availability
risks.note: BRSR flags climate change as a material risk: rising temperatures and extreme weather can disrupt operations, supply chains and raw material availability. Vegetable oils, the industry's key raw materials, are crop-derived, so floods, cyclones and droughts can hit availability, introduce raw material price volatility, influence farmers' decisions and affect production facilities and customer demand. Mitigation is described as strengthening sustainable sourcing by partnering with key suppliers.

risks.risk: Raw material and energy cost fluctuation compressing chemical-industry margins
risks.note: The MD&A notes the chemicals industry saw mixed regional trends, with demand improving gradually in select end-user industries but margin pressures persisting due to fluctuations in raw material and energy costs.

risks.risk: Geopolitical fragmentation, trade disruption and logistics cost
risks.note: The outlook is stated to be influenced by significant external risks including geopolitical fragmentation, trade disruptions and evolving energy dynamics; continued geopolitical tensions may disrupt key trade routes, increase logistics costs and require tighter financial conditions for longer.

risks.risk: Moderating demand and tighter monetary conditions in advanced economies
risks.note: Growth momentum across advanced economies moderated on tighter monetary policy and softer consumer demand, and inflation is expected to tick up in FY 2026 before easing in FY 2027 — relevant given the Company's export orientation.

BRSR discloses that exports contribute 54.64% of total turnover, so more than half the business is exposed to overseas demand cycles, trade policy and currency volatility, which the MD&A separately notes affected India's external sector.

risks.risk: Regulatory dependence of the growth thesis on environmental standards
risks.note: Demand growth is described as being accelerated by sustainability-led regulation in Europe and North America (including REACH) shifting users away from petrochemical-based inputs; the pace of bio-based adoption is therefore tied to the continuation of those regulatory frameworks.

one-line thesis: FY26 was another **flat-growth, full-capacity year** (revenue +4.3%, PAT +1.6%, EBITDA margin compressed to 20.4% from 22.6% in FY25) — management has explicitly pre-announced that **FY27 will also be flat** since every existing plant is running at full utilization and no new capacity comes on until the JNPA-SEZ (H2FY28) and US Phase-1 (18–24 months post construction-start, not yet begun) commission. The quarter's real news is optionality-building: an 80% Malaysia acquisition (Oleofine Organics/OFM, ~₹54cr revenue), a new Dubai subsidiary for GCC reach, and confirmation that raw-material (palm/vegetable oil) inflation — driven by Indonesia/Malaysia biodiesel mandates and the West Asia conflict — will persist through FY27.

> One-offs called out by mgmt: ~₹7cr one-time gratuity provision (new labour codes) inflating employee costs — ex this, underlying employee-cost growth still ~15% YoY on ~4% revenue growth, driven by strategic SEZ-project hiring (training ahead of plant readiness). Depreciation jumped QoQ (₹14cr Q3FY26 → ₹18cr Q4FY26, ~25%) — mgmt attributes this to **IND-AS lease-accounting adjustments + capitalization of R&D expansion/new corporate office/warehouses, NOT new production capacity** — flagged explicitly so it isn't misread as a capacity signal.
guidance (critical — verify next quarter:
- Revenue growth: **explicitly flat for FY27** ("even next year is going to be flat... I cannot add any additional capacity... so one more year is going to be flat") — no meaningful top-line growth until SEZ/US commission; any apparent growth will be price-led, not volume.
- Margin: sustainable EBITDA band reiterated at **18–20%**, based on 10-year historical track record; mgmt says this should hold "even in the worst situation" provided RM prices don't go "totally completely out of control."
- Order book / inflow target: none given (recurring policy).
- Capex / commissioning: **JNPA SEZ** — total ₹700–750cr over 18–24 months (bulk in Phase 1, some base-building for Phase 2); commercial production **now guided to second half of FY28** (was "sometime in FY28"); SEZ subsidiary total investment to date ~₹192.5cr (incl. ₹65cr preference shares issued in FY26); CWIP not yet meaningfully up — contractors only recently onboarded, advances just released, "meaningful number... in the coming quarters."
- **US plant**: still no capex figure — "probably within next quarter" (Q1FY27 call) once contractor negotiations finalize; construction **not yet started**; commissioning targeted **18–24 months from construction start** (mgmt "will try for 18 months"); Phase 1 deliberately conservative (first-time US operations, wholly owned, no JV) with Phase 2/3 "much bigger"; import tariff impact settled at an acceptable 10–15% (down from an initial 50% scare).
- **Malaysia (OFM)**: 80% stake acquisition (50% from promoter-group entity Smoothex Chemicals Pvt Ltd, 30% from other OFM shareholders) at aggregate ~MYR 34.2mn (~₹82.9cr); OFM FY-ended-Jan-2026 revenue **~₹54cr** (mgmt corrected an on-call "₹40-odd/₹44cr" misstatement twice); deal to close within ~3 months; product line currently 100% palm-based food additives, exports mainly to Asia (Indonesia, China, Vietnam, Pakistan) — no US exposure planned even post-expansion.
- **Dubai/UAE subsidiary**: newly incorporated in FY26 for GCC market access; AED 200,000 (~₹49.5 lakh) equity infused in Q4FY26 — sales-office scale only, no manufacturing.
- **Thailand JV**: additional equity of ~₹6.17cr (THB 22.5mn) infused in FY26 to support growth; JV running at full capacity but expansion **on hold** until the SEZ project team frees up (explicitly de-prioritized behind JNPA and US).
order book & pipeline: Not disclosed (company policy, recurring across quarters).
segment / subsidiary detail: Patalganga facility (commissioned for food additives) ramping steadily, expected to reach full capacity in FY27. All existing manufacturing facilities running at "almost full/full" utilization through FY26. Domestic vs export split not re-quantified this call (FY25 call: domestic 43%/8–10% CAGR, export 57%). During capacity-constrained periods, domestic customers get supply priority over export customers (mgmt says this pre-agreed with export customers ~2 years in advance). Feed nutrition division (launched 2018–19 with one product) now has 14–15 commercialized products — cited as the template for how new-product optionality slowly compounds.
growth verticals / optionality: US manufacturing (Phase 1 of 3; 160 acres acquired in Jonesville, Union County, South Carolina; construction not started, contractor finalization ongoing; product approvals for existing exported lines already in place, so Phase-1 risk is mainly execution, not regulatory); Malaysia (OFM) acquisition as a strategic palm-feedstock/Asian-export foothold, explicitly framed as a platform for future sizable expansion, not a near-term earnings driver; Dubai subsidiary for GCC distribution efficiency; Thailand JV expansion (paused, queued behind SEZ/US); continuing R&D pipeline (new applications in beauty/personal-care, animal feed) with multi-year (2–4 yr) regulatory-to-commercial gestation; co-development/NDA projects with large customers (custom-tailored additives).
6a. moat & competitive position:
- **Niche performance-additive positioning, not commodity**: products used at 0.1–0.5% dosage as functional/performance additives — mgmt notes zero evidence of customers dropping usage or going bankrupt despite price increases, because the product is not fungible on price.
- **Differentiated from large conglomerate peers**: Kerry (large Irish dairy/food conglomerate) only overlaps with FINEORG in one small emulsifier line — not a true peer; Palsgaard (140-year-old Nordic specialist, confectionery-focused) is the closer peer/benchmark — mutual-learning relationship, "you can connect us more with Palsgaard rather than Kerry."
- **Global regulatory-approval stock as a switching-cost moat**: existing products already carry global approvals across large, medium and small domestic/export customers; only genuinely new products require fresh regulatory + customer approval — this is why the SEZ's first-phase output (transferring already-exported/approved products) needs no fresh approval cycle, de-risking the ramp.
- **Historical crisis-management edge**: cited FY23 (post-COVID) outperformance vs US/Europe competitors as evidence of superior raw-material stocking/inventory discipline during supply-chain shocks.
margins & cost dynamics: FY26 EBITDA margin 20.4% vs 22.6% FY25 — RM prices "marginally" higher in Q4FY26 vs Q3FY26; freight costs, largely stable through most of FY26, rose in Q4FY26 due to West Asia conflict-driven port disruptions in the Middle East (customers rerouting via partially operating ports + road, but customers bear the incremental freight as FOB buyers — no direct FINEORG margin hit cited from freight specifically). Palm/vegetable oil inflation driven by biodiesel diversion (Indonesia mandating up to 50% palm-oil blending, Malaysia at 15% and rising) expected to keep RM prices elevated through FY27 ("we have to be a little careful in FY27"). Company has shifted to short-term (1–3 month) customer contracts given price volatility, rather than long-term fixed contracts — a deliberate risk-management stance, not a sign of demand weakness. Mgmt reiterates 18–20% EBITDA margin as the sustainable through-cycle band (based on 10-year history), with FY22–23 (~"best year", post-COVID stocking advantage) explicitly flagged as a non-repeatable outlier, not a benchmark.
capex / expansion (watch slippage): FY26 capex not separately itemized this call (FY25 call: ₹125cr consol., ₹110cr of which was SEZ land). JNPA SEZ: ₹700–750cr total (18–24 months), commissioning **pushed/clarified to H2FY28**; CWIP has not yet meaningfully built up despite subsidiary funding — mgmt flags contractor onboarding and advance payments only recently started, so the ramp in reported capex/CWIP should show "in the coming quarters." US plant: land acquired (160 acres), construction not started, capex figure deferred to Q1FY27 call. Historical precedent risk flagged by mgmt itself: a prior Gujarat (Dholera, 100 acres) land acquisition was delayed >1 year and ultimately denied by the state government (policy reservation for semiconductors/autos), pushing FINEORG's expansion timeline back 1–1.5 years — offered as context for why the current capex program is phased/conservative rather than front-loaded.
capital allocation: FY26 uses: SEZ subsidiary funding (₹65cr preference shares issued in FY26, cumulative subsidiary investment ~₹192.5cr to date); US equity infusion ~USD1.12mn (~₹9.6cr) plus land acquisition; Dubai equity ~₹49.5 lakh; Thailand JV additional equity ~₹6.17cr; Malaysia (OFM) acquisition ~₹82.9cr (cash consideration, expected to close within 3 months) — funded via cash/internal accruals, debt "to supplement" where needed. Cash/net-debt position not updated this call (last disclosed FY25: net cash ~₹1,150–1,200cr).
risks & watch-items:
- Raw-material (palm/vegetable oil) inflation likely to persist through FY27, driven by biodiesel diversion mandates and the ongoing West Asia conflict/crude-price linkage — explicit management caution.
- Two consecutive flat-growth years already pre-guided (FY26 done, FY27 also flat) — no re-rating catalyst until SEZ (H2FY28)/US commissioning.
- SEZ CWIP not yet showing meaningful build-up — execution/timeline slippage risk on the H2FY28 target given work has only just started on-ground.
- US project: no capex figure yet, construction not started, first-time US manufacturing/operational execution risk explicitly flagged by mgmt as the main (not regulatory) risk.
- Land-acquisition/regulatory delay precedent (Gujarat/Dholera denial) — a repeat risk factor for JNPA/US site execution.
- Ammonia (critical input for several product categories) in tight global supply — no disruption experienced yet, but mgmt flags potential impact "if this war prolongs further."
- Short-term (1–3 month) customer contracts reduce revenue visibility versus prior longer-term arrangements.
- West Asia conflict — Middle East port disruptions/freight volatility; geopolitical/currency risk in export markets broadly.
management quality / tone: Candid and consistent: mgmt had already told investors ahead of time that FY26 and FY27 would both be flat years due to full capacity utilization, and reiterated this unprompted when challenged by an investor (Bharat Shah) on long-term growth trends. Transparent about mistakes — openly narrates the Gujarat/Dholera land-acquisition failure as a cautionary, unprompted disclosure. Corrects its own on-call errors proactively (OFM/Oleofine revenue restated from ~₹44cr to ~₹54cr, twice, via transcript notes). Deliberately withholds specific capacity/revenue figures for the US and SEZ plants citing competitive sensitivity ("not in the interest of the company"), while still answering directionally. Conservative/phased posture on US entry explicitly framed as risk management given zero prior US operating experience.
non-obvious takeaways:
- The FY27 "flat" guidance was **not new information given reactively** — management says it had already communicated this to investors well before this call; the market should not be surprised by continued flat growth through FY28.
- OFM (Malaysia) is financially trivial (~₹54cr revenue, ballpark ~₹10cr EBITDA at a hypothetical 20% margin) against FINEORG's ~₹2,365cr topline — it's a strategic feedstock/geography optionality bet (palm-oil-producing-country presence, Asian export base), not a near-term earnings driver, despite being labeled an "important" acquisition.
- SEZ CWIP lagging investment-to-date (~₹192.5cr in the subsidiary) is a genuine yellow flag on pacing versus the H2FY28 commissioning target — mgmt's own answer ("advances have been released, but this has happened very recently") suggests the visible on-ground ramp is only starting now.
- The QoQ depreciation jump (₹14cr → ₹18cr) is accounting-driven (IND-AS lease treatment + non-production capitalization: R&D, corporate office, warehouses) — explicitly NOT a signal of new commercial capacity, worth flagging so it isn't misread in screens.
- Employee cost growth (~15% YoY ex the ₹7cr one-off gratuity provision) is front-loaded strategic hiring for the SEZ project (training staff ahead of plant readiness) — mgmt guided this pace to continue similarly in FY27, i.e. opex growth will outrun revenue growth for at least one more year.

Feed nutrition division (launched 2018–19 with one product) now has 14–15 commercialized products — cited as the template for how new-product optionality slowly compounds.
growth verticals / optionality: US manufacturing (Phase 1 of 3; 160 acres acquired in Jonesville, Union County, South Carolina; construction not started, contractor finalization ongoing; product approvals for existing exported lines already in place, so Phase-1 risk is mainly execution, not regulatory); Malaysia (OFM) acquisition as a strategic palm-feedstock/Asian-export foothold, explicitly framed as a platform for future sizable expansion, not a near-term earnings driver; Dubai subsidiary for GCC distribution efficiency; Thailand JV expansion (paused, queued behind SEZ/US); continuing R&D pipeline (new applications in beauty/personal-care, animal feed) with multi-year (2–4 yr) regulatory-to-commercial gestation; co-development/NDA projects with large customers (custom-tailored additives).
6a. moat & competitive position:
- **Niche performance-additive positioning, not commodity**: products used at 0.1–0.5% dosage as functional/performance additives — mgmt notes zero evidence of customers dropping usage or going bankrupt despite price increases, because the product is not fungible on price.
- **Differentiated from large conglomerate peers**: Kerry (large Irish dairy/food conglomerate) only overlaps with FINEORG in one small emulsifier line — not a true peer; Palsgaard (140-year-old Nordic specialist, confectionery-focused) is the closer peer/benchmark — mutual-learning relationship, "you can connect us more with Palsgaard rather than Kerry."
- **Global regulatory-approval stock as a switching-cost moat**: existing products already carry global approvals across large, medium and small domestic/export customers; only genuinely new products require fresh regulatory + customer approval — this is why the SEZ's first-phase output (transferring already-exported/approved products) needs no fresh approval cycle, de-risking the ramp.
- **Historical crisis-management edge**: cited FY23 (post-COVID) outperformance vs US/Europe competitors as evidence of superior raw-material stocking/inventory discipline during supply-chain shocks.
margins & cost dynamics: FY26 EBITDA margin 20.4% vs 22.6% FY25 — RM prices "marginally" higher in Q4FY26 vs Q3FY26; freight costs, largely stable through most of FY26, rose in Q4FY26 due to West Asia conflict-driven port disruptions in the Middle East (customers rerouting via partially operating ports + road, but customers bear the incremental freight as FOB buyers — no direct FINEORG margin hit cited from freight specifically). Palm/vegetable oil inflation driven by biodiesel diversion (Indonesia mandating up to 50% palm-oil blending, Malaysia at 15% and rising) expected to keep RM prices elevated through FY27 ("we have to be a little careful in FY27"). Company has shifted to short-term (1–3 month) customer contracts given price volatility, rather than long-term fixed contracts — a deliberate risk-management stance, not a sign of demand weakness. Mgmt reiterates 18–20% EBITDA margin as the sustainable through-cycle band (based on 10-year history), with FY22–23 (~"best year", post-COVID stocking advantage) explicitly flagged as a non-repeatable outlier, not a benchmark.
capex / expansion (watch slippage): FY26 capex not separately itemized this call (FY25 call: ₹125cr consol., ₹110cr of which was SEZ land). JNPA SEZ: ₹700–750cr total (18–24 months), commissioning **pushed/clarified to H2FY28**; CWIP has not yet meaningfully built up despite subsidiary funding — mgmt flags contractor onboarding and advance payments only recently started, so the ramp in reported capex/CWIP should show "in the coming quarters." US plant: land acquired (160 acres), construction not started, capex figure deferred to Q1FY27 call. Historical precedent risk flagged by mgmt itself: a prior Gujarat (Dholera, 100 acres) land acquisition was delayed >1 year and ultimately denied by the state government (policy reservation for semiconductors/autos), pushing FINEORG's expansion timeline back 1–1.5 years — offered as context for why the current capex program is phased/conservative rather than front-loaded.
capital allocation: FY26 uses: SEZ subsidiary funding (₹65cr preference shares issued in FY26, cumulative subsidiary investment ~₹192.5cr to date); US equity infusion ~USD1.12mn (~₹9.6cr) plus land acquisition; Dubai equity ~₹49.5 lakh; Thailand JV additional equity ~₹6.17cr; Malaysia (OFM) acquisition ~₹82.9cr (cash consideration, expected to close within 3 months) — funded via cash/internal accruals, debt "to supplement" where needed. Cash/net-debt position not updated this call (last disclosed FY25: net cash ~₹1,150–1,200cr).
risks & watch-items:
- Raw-material (palm/vegetable oil) inflation likely to persist through FY27, driven by biodiesel diversion mandates and the ongoing West Asia conflict/crude-price linkage — explicit management caution.
- Two consecutive flat-growth years already pre-guided (FY26 done, FY27 also flat) — no re-rating catalyst until SEZ (H2FY28)/US commissioning.
- SEZ CWIP not yet showing meaningful build-up — execution/timeline slippage risk on the H2FY28 target given work has only just started on-ground.
- US project: no capex figure yet, construction not started, first-time US manufacturing/operational execution risk explicitly flagged by mgmt as the main (not regulatory) risk.
- Land-acquisition/regulatory delay precedent (Gujarat/Dholera denial) — a repeat risk factor for JNPA/US site execution.
- Ammonia (critical input for several product categories) in tight global supply — no disruption experienced yet, but mgmt flags potential impact "if this war prolongs further."
- Short-term (1–3 month) customer contracts reduce revenue visibility versus prior longer-term arrangements.
- West Asia conflict — Middle East port disruptions/freight volatility; geopolitical/currency risk in export markets broadly.
management quality / tone: Candid and consistent: mgmt had already told investors ahead of time that FY26 and FY27 would both be flat years due to full capacity utilization, and reiterated this unprompted when challenged by an investor (Bharat Shah) on long-term growth trends. Transparent about mistakes — openly narrates the Gujarat/Dholera land-acquisition failure as a cautionary, unprompted disclosure. Corrects its own on-call errors proactively (OFM/Oleofine revenue restated from ~₹44cr to ~₹54cr, twice, via transcript notes). themes.title: Import-substitution / China+1 specialty chemicals
themes.need: After the worst agrochem/chemicals year in living memory, the cycle is turning on China+1 reshoring and global pigment/dye consolidation. SUDARSCHEM is now #2 global pigment player post-Heubach; SUMICHEM posted record FY26 margins; AETHER/ANURAS/DEEPAKNTR/CLEAN add CRAMS + backward-integration; war-driven RM/freight inflation is being passed through. Q1FY27 shows the reshoring build-out actually landing: HSCL grew consolidated revenue 28% to INR 1,432cr with PAT INR 228cr (+27%) at a 22% EBITDA margin while opening three new value ladders in a single quarter (carbon nanotube 200 MTPA by Q4FY27, super-speciality carbon black 6,000 MTPA by FY28, and India's first commercial anthraquinone/carbazole plant), all self-funded with no incremental debt; TATVA grew revenue 43% YoY and delivered its first commercial-plant-scale semiconductor batch, qualified by the customer and called 'the glaring achievement of the past decade' (though commercialisation is explicitly not before Q4 CY2028); FCL tripled total income to INR 386.72cr (+165%) with Texas capacity nearly doubled to 148,000 MTPA and already running 63% on a single shift, so its next revenue leg needs only USD 1-2mn of capex.
themes.driver: Volume rebound as destocking ends; price hikes sticking; new value-ladder commissioning (HSCL CNT/carbon black) and semiconductor-materials qualification (TATVA).

one_liner.title: One Liner (RHP)
one_liner.body: Fine Organics Industries Limited is a global manufacturer of performance speciality additives built on green, plant-based chemistry that replaces conventional synthetic alternatives across food, polymer, personal care and feed applications.

business_model.title: What they do
business_model.body: Fine Organics manufactures performance speciality additives derived almost entirely from sustainable, plant-based feedstock, supplying critical ingredients to manufacturers across diverse industries. Its technologically advanced portfolio spans high-performance food emulsifiers, advanced polymer additives, premium personal care ingredients and highly specialised feed nutrition solutions, each purpose-built to solve a specific manufacturing challenge such as improving processing efficiency in bioplastics, enhancing texture and mouthfeel while maintaining clean-label standards, or improving the safety and sustainability profile of end-user products. The Company exports its solutions worldwide and supports them through an integrated network of regional distributors and specialised technical support teams.

segment_detail.body: Patalganga facility (commissioned for food additives) ramping steadily, expected to reach full capacity in FY27. During capacity-constrained periods, domestic customers get supply priority over export customers (mgmt says this pre-agreed with export customers ~2 years in advance). products.body:

- **Polymer additives:** Advanced polymer additives
- **Personal care:** Premium personal care ingredients
- **Feed nutrition:** Highly specialised feed nutrition solutions
- **Specialty additives:** Ink additives, Wires and cables additives, Lubricant additives

- Animal feed nutrition and pet care

guidance.title: Guidance (CRITICAL — verify next quarter)
guidance.body:
- Revenue growth: **explicitly flat for FY27** ("even next year is going to be flat... I cannot add any additional capacity... so one more year is going to be flat") — no meaningful top-line growth until SEZ/US commission; any apparent growth will be price-led, not volume.
- Margin: sustainable EBITDA band reiterated at **18–20%**, based on 10-year historical track record; mgmt says this should hold "even in the worst situation" provided RM prices don't go "totally completely out of control."
- Order book / inflow target: none given (recurring policy).
- Capex / commissioning: **JNPA SEZ** — total ₹700–750cr over 18–24 months (bulk in Phase 1, some base-building for Phase 2); commercial production **now guided to second half of FY28** (was "sometime in FY28"); SEZ subsidiary total investment to date ~₹192.5cr (incl. ₹65cr preference shares issued in FY26); CWIP not yet meaningfully up — contractors only recently onboarded, advances just released, "meaningful number... in the coming quarters."
- **US plant**: still no capex figure — "probably within next quarter" (Q1FY27 call) once contractor negotiations finalize; construction **not yet started**; commissioning targeted **18–24 months from construction start** (mgmt "will try for 18 months"); Phase 1 deliberately conservative (first-time US operations, wholly owned, no JV) with Phase 2/3 "much bigger"; import tariff impact settled at an acceptable 10–15% (down from an initial 50% scare).
- **Malaysia (OFM)**: 80% stake acquisition (50% from promoter-group entity Smoothex Chemicals Pvt Ltd, 30% from other OFM shareholders) at aggregate ~MYR 34.2mn (~₹82.9cr); OFM FY-ended-Jan-2026 revenue **~₹54cr** (mgmt corrected an on-call "₹40-odd/₹44cr" misstatement twice); deal to close within ~3 months; product line currently 100% palm-based food additives, exports mainly to Asia (Indonesia, China, Vietnam, Pakistan) — no US exposure planned even post-expansion.
- **Dubai/UAE subsidiary**: newly incorporated in FY26 for GCC market access; AED 200,000 (~₹49.5 lakh) equity infused in Q4FY26 — sales-office scale only, no manufacturing.
- **Thailand JV**: additional equity of ~₹6.17cr (THB 22.5mn) infused in FY26 to support growth; JV running at full capacity but expansion **on hold** until the SEZ project team frees up (explicitly de-prioritized behind JNPA and US).

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- Global transition towards safer materials, circular production and responsible sourcing is described as accelerating and irreversible, moving biodegradable and bio-based additives from niche to mainstream adoption across food, polymers, personal care, feeds and coatings
- Customers across industries are actively reformulating products to meet stricter safety and sustainability standards, reinforcing long-term demand for the Company's solutions
- Vegetable oil prices remained volatile on weather, supply concentration and competing food/energy demand, creating a cost cycle distinct from petrochemical-based alternatives
- Freight costs remained elevated during the year, managed through supply chain optimisation, efficiency gains and the global network to protect export competitiveness
- Most manufacturing facilities operated at near to full capacity through the year despite persistent input cost pressures
- Disciplined procurement, strategic inventory management and agile pricing mechanisms agreed with customers were used to absorb agricultural commodity volatility
- IMF April 2026 WEO projects global growth to slow to 3.1% in 2026 before stabilising to 3.2% in FY 2027, with inflation ticking up in FY 2026 before easing in FY 2027
- Global specialty chemicals market expected to grow at a CAGR of approximately 5.1%, with Asia-Pacific the primary growth driver
- Indian specialty chemicals market estimated at US$ 67.0 billion in FY 2025, shifting from a cost-driven base to a value-added, innovation-led ecosystem
- End-users increasingly willing to pay a premium for advanced additives delivering superior functionality at lower dosage with a reduced environmental footprint
- Global supply chain de-risking is redirecting procurement towards transparent, reliable alternative manufacturing hubs, with emphasis on supply security, IP protection and ethical ESG sourcing over pure cost
- Regulatory pushes — REACH in Europe, single-use plastic phase-outs and EPR mandates in India, clean-label demand in food and clean-beauty standards in personal care — are structurally expanding demand for bio-based additives
- Indian demand supported by food processing modernisation, QSR and cloud-kitchen expansion into Tier 2/Tier 3 cities, e-commerce-driven packaging, infrastructure-linked PVC and cable demand, and premiumisation in personal care

other.body:
- [Insurance claim closed] Following the fire incident on 18 January 2024 at a neighbouring facility, which damaged certain property, plant and equipment and inventories and temporarily disrupted operations, the business interruption claim of Rs 6.98 crore was settled in Q1 FY26 (recognised as an exceptional item), and in July 2026 the property damage and inventory loss claim was 'finally settled at Rs 4.35 crore', against interim settlements aggregating Rs 1.80 crore already received in earlier periods; adjustments have been incorporated in the standalone financial statements for the quarter ended 30 June.
- [Board change] Shailendra Nadkarni joined as Independent Director in 2026, 'with effect from May 19, 2026, subject to shareholders' approval in the Annual General Meeting of the Company'; Rashi Mehta joined in 2024.
- [Geopolitical exposure] The ongoing West Asia geopolitical crisis is named as the direct driver of higher fuel and therefore utility costs.
- [Two reporting entities] Standalone and consolidated results differ materially in gross margin (FY26 gross profit margin 36.4% standalone vs 40.1% consolidated) and the consolidated numbers absorb a share of loss of joint ventures (Rs -3.1 crore in FY26), so figures must be read at the level the deck labels them.
